result:
I've been thinking about how cities breathe at night. Not metaphorically, but literally. The exhale of air conditioners, the inhale of traffic slowing down. At 2 a.m., my apartment building settles into a different frequency. The pipes stop knocking. The neighbor's TV goes quiet. It is the only time I can hear the refrigerator hum properly, like a low cello note.

I used to hate nights like this because they made me feel exposed. Now I like them. I keep a chipped mug on the windowsill and watch the streetlights turn the rain into a thin silver curtain. No one is pretending to be busy. The delivery bikes are gone. The convenience store is shuttered.

People say you need silence to think, but I think you need a little noise to remember you are alive. The city gives you both. One minute it's a roar, the next it's a held breath.

Sometimes I write lists on the back of receipts. Things I will do, things I have done. Most of them are small and reversible. Buy better coffee. Call my sister. Learn the name of the moth that lives in the hallway light.

It feels honest, this small inventory. Not a plan, just a record of attention.

I don't know where any of this leads. Maybe nowhere. But at 2 a.m., with the building breathing around me, it feels enough to be awake while the rest of the world rehearses for morning. That is the whole point.
